summary: Updates how trustees of the IETF Trust are selected. Because the IAOC was eliminated, its members no longer double as trustees, so trustees are chosen separately. Everything else about the Trust is unchanged. It obsoletes RFC 4371.

plainLanguage.summary: Before, the same people did two jobs. Now the trustees who look after the IETF's stuff are picked on their own.

questions: how many trustees does the ietf trust have
subtitle: Why the IETF Trust's five trustees are now picked on their own instead of coming from a defunct oversight committee.

tldr.problem: The IETF Trust's trustees used to be drawn from the members of the IAOC, but the IAOC was eliminated in an update to the IASA structure, so that rule no longer worked.
tldr.mechanism: The Trust gets five trustees chosen separately: three appointed by the NomCom and confirmed by the IESG, one appointed by the IESG and one appointed by the ISOC Board of Trustees, all on staggered terms.
tldr.outcome: Only trustee selection changes; everything else about the Trust stays as it was. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4371.

today: RFC 8714 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 4371. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Trustee Selection Changes
sections.content:
RFC 8714 updates the process for selecting Trustees of the IETF Trust. Previously, members of the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) also acted as Trustees. The IAOC has been eliminated as part of an update to the structure of the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA), so the old arrangement had to change.

The memo obsoletes RFC 4371. The changes relate only to the selection of Trustees; all other aspects of the IETF Trust remain as they are. The reasoning behind the change is left to RFC 8715.
sections.plainLanguage: A club used to pick its helpers from one committee. The committee was closed, so the club needed a new way to choose them.

sections.title: What the IETF Trust Is
sections.content:
The RFC copies the definition of the Trust from RFC 4371, leaving out the part about Trustee selection and adding a pointer to the IETF Trust website. The Trust was formed to acquire, hold, maintain and license certain existing and future intellectual property and other property used in connection with the administration of the IETF.

The Trust was formed by the signatures of its Settlors and initial Trustees. The Settlors, who contributed the initial intellectual property, were ISOC and the Corporation for National Research Initiatives. The Beneficiary of the IETF Trust is the IETF as a whole.
sections.plainLanguage: The Trust is like a safe box that holds things the IETF uses, such as its rights to certain written works. It is kept for the benefit of everyone in the IETF.

sections.title: Five Trustees from Three Sources
sections.content:
This document revises the Trustee selection procedures originally defined in RFC 4071 and RFC 4371 to remove the requirement that Trustees be drawn from the members of the IAOC.

In the new structure there are five Trustees. Three are appointed by the IETF Nominating Committee (NomCom) and confirmed by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). One is appointed by the IESG, and one by the Internet Society (ISOC) Board of Trustees. The appointments by the IESG and the ISOC Board of Trustees do not require confirmation.

The IETF Trust Chair tells the nominating committee which Trustee positions are up for review. The Trust also gives each appointing body a summary of the expertise it wants in candidates.
sections.plainLanguage: Five helpers look after the box. Different groups each choose some of them, so no single group picks everyone.

sections.title: Terms of Office
sections.content:
Trustees appointed by the NomCom serve three-year terms. To stagger them, the initial selection is for one, two and three year terms. The IESG and ISOC Board of Trustees appointments are two-year terms, with the initial terms being one year and two years, respectively. The stated goal is to minimize potential Trustee turnover in any single year.

To keep the terms staggered, an appointing body may, at its discretion, appoint Trustees for shorter terms in exceptional situations, for example for mid-term vacancies or when an appointment is not ready by the time of the first IETF meeting of the year.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers do not all start and finish on the same day. That way the box is never left with only brand new helpers.

sections.title: Chair, Recall and Rollout
sections.content:
Once the initial selections are done, and at each later annual meeting of the Trust (after new Trustees are seated), the Trustees elect one of themselves as IETF Trust Chair by a majority vote.

NomCom-appointed Trustees can be recalled using the process in BCP 10 (RFC 8713). Trustees appointed by the IESG or by the ISOC Board can be recalled by the appointing body. For IESG appointments, the IESG is expected to run an open selection process and to consider the necessary skills and conflicts of interest.

Putting this into effect needs a change to the Trust Agreement. The document asks the current Trustees to make it at the earliest convenient time and no later than the end of the 104th IETF meeting in March 2019.
sections.plainLanguage: The helpers vote for a leader, and whoever chose a helper can usually send them home again if things go wrong.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that it has no security implications for the Internet. It also has no IANA actions, because it concerns how an organization picks its Trustees and not any protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: This is about who picks the helpers, not about computers talking, so nothing about network safety changes.
